analysis.one_liner: Bans evictions and federally backed mortgage foreclosures in federally declared disaster areas for limited periods.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in August 2021 but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a federally declared disaster or emergency, this bill would have paused evictions for nonpayment of rent for 90 days and blocked foreclosures on federally backed mortgages for six months, except for vacant or abandoned homes. Landlords could not raise rent, charge late fees, refuse to let displaced tenants return, or refuse to renew a lease during that period, and they would have to tell tenants about federal disaster assistance they might qualify for. It applies to any disaster declared on or after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and homeowners in areas hit by a federally declared disaster. Renters get a 90-day shield against eviction filings, late fees, rent hikes, and refusal to renew leases after a disaster, plus written notice of FEMA and Small Business Administration help. Homeowners with federally backed mortgages (most loans involving FHA, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac) get six months without foreclosure activity, giving them time to repair, rebuild, or work out payment plans while recovering from the disaster.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and homeowners in disaster areas

how_it_helps.text: Renters in a disaster area cannot be taken to court for nonpayment of rent, charged late fees, hit with rent increases, blocked from returning after temporary relocation, or refused a lease renewal during a 90-day moratorium period.
A landlord cannot issue a notice to vacate until after the moratorium period ends, and once issued, the tenant gets at least 30 days before having to leave.

Servicers of federally backed mortgages cannot start foreclosure, seek a judgment or sale, or conduct a foreclosure-related eviction for six months after a disaster is declared, unless the property is vacant or abandoned.
Landlords must notify tenants of damage assessment status and disaster assistance available from FEMA and the Small Business Administration, for which either party may be eligible.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and mortgage servicers. Renters still owe the rent that accrues during the moratorium, and landlords cannot collect it, charge late fees, or raise rents to cover it during the period. Small landlords without reserves would bear this cost without compensation. Mortgage servicers would carry loans that would otherwise have moved to foreclosure for an extra six months.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium pauses eviction and foreclosure but does not cancel the debt: rent and mortgage payments accrue during the protected period and come due afterward, which can leave households owing a large back-payment lump sum once protection expires.

Landlords, including small landlords with thin margins, absorb the cost of unpaid rent, waived late fees, and frozen rents during the moratorium, with no compensation or relief fund provided in the bill.

Rent freezes and eviction bans during a disaster can discourage some landlords from maintaining or renting units in disaster-prone regions, since a declared disaster freezes their income while their costs continue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the target population — people whose homes and livelihoods were just wrecked by a disaster — a temporary shield against losing their housing is a significant benefit at a modest cost: payments are deferred, not erased, and the protection lasts 90 days for renters and six months for federally backed mortgages. The main weakness is on the landlord side: small landlords absorb real costs with no offsetting relief, and accrued arrears can hit tenants hard when the moratorium lifts. The foreclosure moratorium only touches federally backed loans, which limits the benefit to a large but not universal share of homeowners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2021 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Demings, with Rep. Al Lawson of Florida, introduced the Federal Disaster Housing Stability Act of 2021 on August 17, 2021.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, which held no hearing, marked it up, or reported it out.
The bill attracted 15 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support during the 117th Congress.
The bill received no floor vote in either chamber and expired with the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and mortgage servicers, who would have faced foreclosure and eviction freezes after disasters, avoided those obligations because the bill never advanced. Renters and homeowners in disaster areas got no new federal protection.

for.name: Rep. Al Lawson of Florida
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only other original sponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred: no hearing, no markup, no report to the House.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would freeze evictions, late fees, and rents in disaster areas for 90 days, cutting landlord revenue precisely when repairs and other costs mount. Small landlords bear this without any compensation, while tenants keep their homes during recovery.

Servicers of federally backed mortgages could not start foreclosure for six months after a disaster declaration, delaying recovery of unpaid balances. Homeowners get breathing room to repair and reorganize their finances.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and other federal mortgage backstops
industries.note: Because the moratorium covers only federally backed loans, the government-sponsored enterprises and federal loan programs would carry delayed foreclosures and unpaid periods — a cost the government absorbs to keep homeowners housed after disasters.
